Gaps searched: build systems, provenance, why-not, Salsa and agent-memory invalidation. Not found: any measurement of recorded-dependency invalidation on code-agent tasks with tokens counted on a real repository.
Most useful results:
1. P4 (quoted, lines 33-52 and 780-806): recording the versions each verdict derives from cut unsafe reuse from 62% to 0.3% of upstream-failing objects and used 37% fewer checks than checking everything. Edges cost 21% more writer tokens. Safety falls with missing edges: edge recall drops to 0.658 when relations are stated two sessions after their verdicts, and unsafe publication rises to 9.4-22.1%. Synthetic worlds, plus 24 real Go advisories; makers' own.
2. P3 (quoted, abstract and lines 595-627): row-level version stamps gave eviction precision 1.00 and 29-33% token saving on 4 of 7 models. Table-level invalidation dropped post-drift first-try to 0% on 5 of 7. Naive memory alone gave 10-28%. The saving needs the model to use the cache: Sonnet 5 complied 11% or less. Synthetic APIs, makers' own.
3. P1 (quoted, lines 664, 681, 1412-1456): early cutoff and verifying traces are defined for deterministic tasks. For non-deterministic ones the correctness definition has to be weakened to "one possible result", and volatile tasks cannot be cached. This is the formal reason a model-made conclusion cannot be cut off by output equality. Salsa says the same (overview line 31).
P5 reports expensive calls per change of 0.18 against 1.00 for full re-run, but its table text is column-garbled, so those numbers are uncertain. P6 (semirings) does not cover negation, so it does not reach "nothing else matches".

No claim was refuted, so no lead was dropped. Leads L2, L5, L7 and L8 were rewritten to use the narrowed claims.

Answer:
1. On a 12 GB card, a 4-bit 8B model (4.58 GiB) fits next to a small reranker, with room for about 56K tokens of cache. Best-evidenced use is a local reader working under the cloud model (MinionS: 97.9 % of the cloud-only accuracy for 18 % of the cloud spend). That result is on documents, not code, and against a baseline that does not cache, so our saving would be smaller.
2. Ranked leads: the local reader (L1), a retriever plus a reranker of 4B or larger (L2), a cascade judged by our own checks (L3), a local executor that calls a cloud expert (L6). Cached re-reads still make up about a fifth of our meter, so the card saves most by removing whole cloud calls or fresh tokens.
3. Negative: a static router that picks the model from the task text, moving the main loop to a local model (fix commits rose from 45.9 % to 74.9 % in the one case), and training on one user's sessions. No source measures any of this on a 12 GB card or in our meter's units.

Gaps searched and not found: cost or tokens by repository size for coding agents; any independent replication of a cost figure. Six candidate titles are listed for later reading.
Most useful results:
1. Harness and scaffold change cost far more than the method does. Claude Code against PI.DEV gives 5-30x higher cost per success at comparable success (wastepr/paper.txt 255-257, quoted, one company, small tasks). HAL reports 9x cost for 2 points of accuracy across two web scaffolds (hal/paper.txt 534-535, quoted, not coding).
2. n=1 per arm is too few, for cost and for success. One task can differ up to 30x in tokens between runs (spendmoney/paper.txt 22-25, quoted). Single-run pass@1 varies 2.2-6.0 points, and a 2-point gain needs about 9 runs per arm at median noise (randomness/paper.txt 16-19, 616-618, quoted).
3. A token count is mostly cache reads and mixes prices. Cache reads are 96-98% of tokens (flowplan/paper.txt 748-749, quoted), and output is priced about 80x a cache read (spendmoney/paper.txt 568-569). Cost per successful task is the unit that joins the seven measures (wastepr, costofpass), and failed attempts cost over 4x a success (sweeffi/paper.txt 84-86).
Caveats: coding cost claims rest on 50-500 public Python tasks, and every figure is the makers' own (self-reported). The paper text has an unresolved inconsistency: Opus 5 low effort 16/25 against 17/25 in wastepr.

**Three most useful results:**
1. **Independent coding tests mostly fail to reproduce makers' gains (quoted).** REM, on SWE-ContextBench Lite with Sonnet 4.5, found that summaries and raw trajectories, even oracle-retrieved, gave no gain: 22-24 of 99 solved against 23 with no memory (`rem/paper.txt` 340-344). The benchmark makers' oracle-summary gain (34.3% vs 26.3%) "does not reproduce" there (23.2% vs 23.2%). REM's own method cut tokens 17% (452K to 374K) but its resolution gain was not significant (McNemar p=0.22).
2. **VibeMemBench (quoted).** Eleven of twelve solver and memory-system pairings do not beat the matched memory-off baseline (`vibemem/paper.txt` 21-26, 446-448). Directly injected, verified experience gave +1.1 to +4.5 points, with every interval crossing zero.
3. **The best measured cost result on coding is EET, and it is self-reported (quoted).** On SWE-bench Verified across six agent-model setups, total cost fell 19.3%-55.1% (mean 31.8%), with resolution loss at most 0.2% (`eet/paper.txt` 378-420). It saves by stopping early, not by reusing a plan. Its cross-repository check was only 50 issues at a 14% solve rate.

**Other findings in the file:**
- **Third-party AWM run (Evo-Memory):** AWM equalled the plain-history baseline on multi-turn tasks (0.30 vs 0.30 on Gemini Flash, 0.49 vs 0.49 on Claude 3.7), but the table rows were read by alignment, so I marked that reasoned.
- **Raw trajectories:** they hurt in STAIR's ablation (80.0% to 57.6%) but cut steps 34% and output tokens 28% in MemDev-Bench.
- **Skills:** they moved the coding pass ratio only from 76.6% to 76.9% in SWE-Skills-Bench. Model-written skills fell 8-11 points below no-skill in SkillsBench.

No card-tier figure exists for any paper; all use hosted models.

Three most useful results (all quoted, all makers' own, none replicated):
1. TokenEconomizer (arXiv 2610.22732) shows cost effects differ by repository. RTK alone raised cost in 12 of 30 repository-setting cells and RepoMap alone in 15. Its own controller cut cost in all 30, by 5.2-40.1%. Source: tokeneco/paper.txt 402-404, 151-152.
2. SWE Context Bench (2602.08316): cache reads are over 97% of tokens. Free retrieval cost $0.98 per instance against $0.79 with no context, a 27.3% increase over the cheapest setting. Summary-based reuse did not cut cost. Source: swectx/paper.txt 429-435.
3. LoLBench (2609.37143), on repositories averaging 2.4 M lines: code localization takes 52.4% of non-cached input tokens, and each attempt uses 1.60 M of them. Source: lolbench/paper.txt 1920-1928.
Also read: Cost-inefficient behaviors (2609.30725) and task-specification token spend (2608.25399).
